newsitem.title: JAPAN: Foreigners increase hold on Japan broking business.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners increase hold on Japan broking business.

text.p: While Japan's stock market is plagued by worries about the country's fragile economic recovery and planned "Big Bang" reforms, foreign brokerages are quietly boosting their presence on the Tokyo bourse.

"Foreigners have always been a large part of the Tokyo stock market," said Masaaki Higashida, deputy general manager at Nomura Securities Co Ltd. "In recent months, their activities have been increasing."
Brokerages such as NatWest Securities Japan Ltd, a unit of Britain's National Westminster Bank Plc, have resumed business in Japan, while others are beefing up their research.

In January, when the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares in Tokyo fell by some six percent due to worries about the economy and bad loans in the banking sector, trading activity of non-residents almost doubled compared with the year before.
Shares traded by 21 foreign brokerages accounted for 27.7 percent of the total, up from 15.1 percent a year earlier, according to data compiled by the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
"The 'Big Four' brokerages are responsible for about 30 percent of trade, but foreigners are slowly catching up," a broker at a Big Four brokerage said.
Brokers attribute the surge in part to greater use of futures by Japanese life insurers and investors to buy and sell cash stocks, which foreign brokers are adept at trading.
Analysts say foreign brokerages may continue to flourish as they have sturdier financial backing than Japanese houses and a head start in derivatives and other complex trading methods.

"There is a limit to just how much more Japanese trading houses can do without strengthening their capital base," said Ayako Sato, an analyst at UBS Securities. "If they can't, it may be difficult for them to compete against foreign brokerages which will keep on employing new tools."
Earnings at Japanese brokerages are still suffering from the collapse of Japan's "bubble" economy in the early 1990s.

Ratings firm Standard & Poor's Corp has revised down three of Japan's Big Four brokerages on the grounds that their capital may diminish as a result of the disposal of bad loans at their financial units. Japan's biggest broker, Nomura Securities Co Ltd, posted a hefty first-half loss.
Firms pressed into eliminating cross-shareholdings ahead of deregulation are also becoming good customers for foreign brokerages.

Once Big Bang deregulation, designed to help Japan catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and North America, gets under way, banks and brokerages will be able to enter each other's sectors.
Cross-shareholding, a traditional practice by which Japanese companies hold each others' shares to strengthen business ties, is losing its sparkle as a result.

"No one wants to be blamed for sending the shares of a certain issue, especially banks, tumbling," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities. "By dispersing sell orders among various foreign brokerages, the confidentiality of the seller can be maintained fairly well."

One consolation for Japanese brokerages is that foreign houses operate in Japan only as wholesalers, brokers said. Domestic securities firms have the retail market so well covered that there is little room for newcomers.

Yoshinobu Yamada, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan, said that in order to survive the competition, Japanese brokerages are moving away from their generalist stance and trying to focus on what they do best, whether retail or wholesale.

"This trend is the opposite of what is happening in the United States," he said. With impending structural changes in brokerage business and Japan a world-class economy, some industry sources said opportunities could eventually emerge for newcomers in the retail market.

On Wednesday, the U.S. giant Morgan Stanley Group unveiled a merger with retail brokerage Dean Witter Discover & Co and analysts said it was possible the merged firm would be interested in the Japanese retail market in future.
Nevertheless, even such big guns may remain unenthusiastic, due to high operating costs and the saturation of the market.

"Brokerage fees are set to be liberalised as a part of the (Big Bang) reforms," said an analyst at a foreign securities houses. "Brokerages, unless they are discount brokerages, will have to think twice before heading into such an environment."
